title: The Ollie Step by Step
bigQuestion: How do a few quick moves, done in the right order, lift a skateboard off flat ground and bring it back under your feet?

story.title: The Carpet in the Garage
story.kicker: Hundreds of tries on a carpet come before the first rolling ollie.
paragraphs: Jordan dragged an old piece of carpet into the garage on the first cold Saturday of fall. The skateboard went on top of it, and its wheels sank into the soft pile. Jordan buckled a helmet, pulled on wrist guards and stood with the back foot on the tail. The board did not roll an inch. That was the point.

The first pops were slow and heavy. The nose rose a little and then thumped back down. Jordan's front foot stayed planted like a brick. A cousin who skated watched for a minute and gave one tip: snap the tail fast, then drag the front shoe up toward the nose. Jordan tried again. The clack of the tail was sharper this time.

By December, a sheet of paper was taped to the garage wall. Each mark on it stood for a clean try, with all four wheels off the carpet and both feet landing over the bolts. The marks crowded into rows of five. Some days the count went up by twenty. Some days it went up by two. The side of Jordan's front shoe wore pale and rough.

In early spring Jordan carried the board to a dry, empty basketball court. Push, roll slowly, set the feet. Crouch, pop, slide, jump, level, land. The board rose a few centimeters and came down under both feet, still rolling. It was a small ollie. It counted. Every mark on that garage wall had been part of it.
story.think: Why might Jordan have practiced on carpet for months before trying an ollie while rolling?

lessons.title: Gear for Ollie Practice
lessons.mainIdea: A buckled helmet that fits, wrist guards, pads and flat shoes let you practice the ollie and fall without serious harm.
reading: Learning the ollie means falling many times, so gear comes before the first try. A *helmet* should sit level on your head, about two finger-widths above your eyebrows. Buckle the chin strap so only one or two fingers fit under it. Shake your head side to side. A helmet that fits stays put and does not slide back to show your forehead.

*Wrist guards* matter because wrist injuries are among the most common skateboarding injuries. When people fall, they reach out with their hands. A wrist guard has a stiff splint that spreads the shock along the forearm. Knee pads and elbow pads let you slide on hard plastic caps instead of skin. Pads that fit snugly stay in place when you land on them.

Shoes matter more for the ollie than for most first tricks. Choose flat shoes with a grippy rubber sole and no raised heel. Running shoes with thick, rounded soles make it hard to feel the board. The ollie rubs the side of the front shoe across rough grip tape, so a sturdy shoe lasts longer. Many skaters see a worn patch on that side of the front shoe after a few weeks.

Gear works best with a plan for falling. If you feel a fall coming, crouch low so you have less distance to drop. Try to roll onto your shoulder or slide on your knee pads. Keep your arms bent and loose. Locked, straight arms send the whole shock into your wrists and elbows.

words.d: a hard shell with foam inside that protects the head; it should fit snugly and be buckled
gloves with a stiff splint that protect the wrists when a skater falls onto the hands

look.title: The Mirror Check
look.text: Stand in front of a mirror with your helmet on. The front edge sits low on your forehead, about two fingers above your eyebrows. The side straps make a V just under each ear. The chin strap is buckled and snug. Now push the front of the helmet up with your palm. If it slides back and shows your whole forehead, the straps need tightening.
look.prompt: Do the push test with your own helmet. What, if anything, did you need to adjust?

check.q: Why do skaters learning the ollie wear wrist guards?
choices: Wrist injuries are among the most common skateboarding injuries
Wrist guards make the board pop higher
Wrist guards keep the hands warm
Wrist guards are needed only in contests
check.why: People reach out with their hands when they fall, and wrist injuries are among the most common in skateboarding. The splint in a wrist guard spreads the shock.

check.q: How should a well-fitted helmet sit?
choices: Tipped back so the forehead shows
Level, about two finger-widths above the eyebrows, with the strap buckled
Loose, so it can turn easily
Unbuckled, so it comes off fast in a fall
check.why: A helmet protects only when it sits level and low on the forehead and the strap is buckled snugly.

check.q: Which is the safest way to fall?
choices: Catch yourself with straight, locked arms
Crouch low and roll or slide on your knee pads
Hold on to the board with both hands
check.why: Crouching lowers the fall, and rolling or sliding spreads the shock. Locked arms send the shock into the wrists and elbows.

lessons.title: A Good Place to Practice
lessons.mainIdea: Practice on a flat, smooth, dry surface away from cars, and start on grass or carpet, where the wheels cannot roll.
reading: The best ollie spot is plain and boring. It is *flat ground*: level, smooth and dry. A quiet basketball court, an empty lot closed to cars, or the flat section of a *skatepark* all work. Wet pavement can make the wheels slip out without warning. Cracks and sand can grab a wheel. Walk the spot first and kick away pebbles, because one small stone can stop a wheel and throw you forward.

Stay far from streets and driveways. A board that shoots out from under you can roll into traffic, and you might chase it without looking. Pick a spot where a loose board stops on grass or against a wall, not in a road. Skateparks are built for practice like this, and many post their own gear rules at the gate.

Your very first ollie practice does not need pavement at all. On thick grass or carpet, the wheels sink in and cannot roll. That lets you learn the motion while the board stays right under you. The board will pop lower on a soft surface, and that is fine. The goal on grass is to learn the order of the moves, not to jump high.

words.d: a level, smooth surface with no ramps, used for practicing tricks such as the ollie
a place built for skateboarding, with ramps, ledges and flat areas

look.title: Two Spots Side by Side
look.text: Spot A is a smooth school blacktop on a dry Saturday, with a fence on one side and grass on the other. Spot B is a sloped driveway that ends at a street, with wet leaves and a few pebbles on it. Picture a board shooting out from under a skater at each spot. At Spot A it rolls into the grass and stops. At Spot B it rolls downhill toward the street.
look.prompt: List three things that make Spot A the safer choice. What would you still check before practicing there?

check.q: Why is a sloped driveway that ends at a street a poor place to practice ollies?
choices: A loose board can roll downhill into the street
check.why: A board that shoots out can roll into traffic. A good spot lets a loose board stop on grass or against a wall.

check.q: Why do learners often start the ollie on grass or carpet?
choices: The wheels sink in and cannot roll, so the board stays under them
check.why: On a soft surface the wheels cannot roll, so a learner can work on the order of the moves while the board stays still.

check.q: What should you do before practicing on a new spot?
choices: Walk it and kick away pebbles and sand
Wet the ground so it grips better
Practice close to the street so friends can see
Lean the board against a parked car
check.why: One small stone can stop a wheel and throw you forward, so clearing the spot first prevents falls.

lessons.title: Where Your Feet Go
lessons.mainIdea: Put the ball of your back foot on the tail and your front foot just behind the front bolts, across the board.
reading: Every ollie starts with the feet in the right place. Look at the top of the deck. Near each end you will see four *bolts*, the screw heads that hold the trucks on. The *tail* is the kicked-up end behind the back bolts. The *nose* is the kicked-up end in front of the front bolts.

Your back foot goes on the tail. Put the ball of your foot, the padded part just behind the toes, near the middle of the tail. Your heel can hang slightly off the edge. Do not stand on the tail with only your toes. The ball of the foot lets you snap down hard and then lift off quickly.

Your front foot goes just behind the front bolts, pointing across the board or angled slightly toward the nose. Leave a gap of about a hand's width behind the bolts, so the foot has room to slide forward. If you ride with your left foot forward, you are *regular*. Right foot forward is *goofy*. Both are normal, which is why skaters say front foot and back foot instead of left and right.

Check your stance by standing on the board on grass. Your feet should be about shoulder-width apart, with your weight even between them. If the nose lifts while you stand still, your back foot is carrying too much weight.

words.d: the screw heads on top of the deck that hold the trucks on; there are four near each end
the kicked-up end of the board behind the back bolts
the kicked-up end of the board in front of the front bolts
riding with the left foot forward
riding with the right foot forward

look.title: A Bird's-Eye View of the Stance
look.text: Look down at a skater standing ready for an ollie. The back foot sits on the tail, the ball of the foot near the middle and the heel hanging just off the edge. The front foot lies across the board a hand's width behind the front bolts. The feet are about as far apart as the shoulders. The nose and tail both rest flat on the ground.
look.prompt: Stand on a board on grass in this stance. Where does your weight feel heaviest, and what would you change to make it even?

check.q: Where does the back foot go for an ollie?
choices: The ball of the foot near the middle of the tail
In the middle of the deck
check.why: The ball of the back foot on the tail lets the skater snap the tail down hard and lift off quickly.

check.q: Where does the front foot start?
choices: Just behind the front bolts, across the board
Off the board, on the ground
check.why: The front foot starts a hand's width behind the front bolts so it has room to slide toward the nose.

check.q: A skater rides with the right foot forward. What is that stance called?
check.why: Right foot forward is goofy and left foot forward is regular. Both are normal stances.

lessons.title: Crouch to Load Your Legs
lessons.mainIdea: Bending your knees low before the pop gives your legs a longer push, so you can jump higher.
reading: Before you pop, you *crouch*. Bend your knees and lower your hips as if you were about to sit in a chair. Keep your back fairly straight and your head up. Your shoulders should line up with the board, pointing toward the nose and the tail. A twisted upper body tends to twist the board too.

The crouch is where the jump's energy starts. A jump is a push against the ground. The lower you bend, the longer your legs can push before your feet leave the board. A longer push sends your body higher. Nobody can jump high from straight legs, and the same is true on a skateboard.

Do not crouch so low that you lose your balance. A good crouch feels springy, not stuck. Your weight stays over the middle of the board, between your feet. If the nose lifts while you crouch, you are leaning back. Move your hips forward until the board sits flat again. Keeping a steady *stance* in the crouch makes every later step easier.

words.d: to bend the knees and lower the body to get ready for a jump
the way a skater stands on the board, including where each foot goes

look.title: A Spring Being Squeezed
look.text: Picture a metal spring standing on a table. Press it halfway down with your hand, then let go, and it jumps a little. Press it all the way down, then let go, and it jumps much higher. Your legs work in a similar way. A deeper crouch lets them push for longer before your feet leave the board.
look.prompt: Try two small jumps on the ground, one from a shallow bend and one from a deep crouch. Which went higher, and why?

check.q: Why do skaters crouch before popping an ollie?
choices: Bending gives the legs a longer push, so the jump goes higher
It keeps the wheels from turning
check.why: The lower you bend, the longer your legs can push against the board, and a longer push sends your body higher.

check.q: Where should your weight be during the crouch?
choices: Over the middle of the board, between your feet
check.why: Weight over the middle keeps the board flat and balanced until the pop.

check.q: While you crouch, the nose lifts off the ground. What does that tell you?
choices: You are leaning back and should move your hips forward
Your front foot is too far back
check.why: A nose that lifts in the crouch means too much weight is behind you, on the tail.

lessons.title: Snap the Tail
lessons.mainIdea: The back foot strikes the tail down hard and fast, the ground pushes back, and the board tips nose-up and rises.
reading: The *pop* is the sound and the move that start every ollie. From the crouch, your back foot snaps the tail down hard and fast so it strikes the ground. You hear a sharp clack. Right after the snap, you lift off the back foot and start to jump. The snap and the jump happen almost together, like one motion.

Here is the science. The board acts as a *lever*, a stiff bar that turns around a point. The back wheels are the *pivot*, the point it turns around. When the tail goes down, the nose swings up. When the tail hits the ground, the ground pushes back up on it. This is Newton's third law: when you push on something, it pushes back on you with an equal force. That push bounces the tail up and lifts the whole board into the air.

A quick snap works better than a slow push. A slow push only tips the board up like a seesaw, and it stays on the ground. A fast snap makes the tail hit the ground and rebound. Think popping, not pressing. If the board barely leaves the ground, snap faster and make sure the ball of your foot strikes the tail.

The trick is named for Alan 'Ollie' Gelfand. In the late 1970s he popped his board into the air without grabbing it while riding the curved walls of ramps and bowls. Skaters began calling the move the ollie. In the early 1980s Rodney Mullen showed it could be done on flat ground. His flat-ground ollie is the version you are learning now.

words.d: snapping the tail hard against the ground so the board bounces up
a stiff bar that turns around a fixed point; pushing one end down lifts the other end
the point a lever turns around; in the ollie, the back wheels

look.title: Newton's Third Law
look.text: To every action there is always opposed an equal reaction: or the mutual actions of two bodies upon each other are always equal, and directed to contrary parts.
look.cite: Isaac Newton, Principia (1687), Law III, in Andrew Motte's English translation (1729)
look.prompt: In the ollie, what is the action and what is the reaction? Name the two bodies that push on each other.

check.q: In the ollie, what acts as the pivot of the lever?
check.why: The board turns around the back wheels: when the tail goes down, the nose swings up.

check.q: What does Newton's third law explain about the pop?
choices: The ground pushes back up on the tail when the tail strikes it
Grip tape keeps the shoe from sliding
check.why: When the tail pushes on the ground, the ground pushes back with an equal force, which bounces the board up.

check.q: Who is the ollie named after?
check.why: Alan 'Ollie' Gelfand popped no-hands airs on ramps and bowls in the late 1970s. Rodney Mullen later took the ollie to flat ground.

lessons.title: Slide the Front Foot Up
lessons.mainIdea: Right after the pop, the front foot drags up the grip tape toward the nose, pulling the board higher.
reading: Right after the pop, your front foot slides forward toward the nose. Roll your front ankle a little so the outside edge of the shoe, the little-toe side, brushes up the board. The foot moves up and forward at the same time. Picture dragging your shoe up a steep hill.

*Grip tape* is the sandpaper-like sheet stuck to the top of the deck. Its rough surface creates a lot of *friction*, a force that resists two surfaces sliding across each other. As your shoe drags upward, friction pulls the board up with it. On a smooth deck with no grip tape, the shoe would slip and the board would drop. That drag is also why the front shoe wears on its side.

Timing matters. Start the slide as soon as the tail pops, not before. If you slide too early, the nose never comes up. If you slide too late, the board rises and then falls back toward the tail. Slide until your front foot reaches the start of the nose's curve. Then get ready to push the nose down.

words.d: a rough, sandpaper-like sheet on top of the deck that keeps shoes from slipping
a force that resists one surface sliding across another

look.title: The Slide in Slow Motion
look.text: Watch an ollie at quarter speed from the side. The tail strikes the ground. The nose tilts up. The front shoe rolls onto its outside edge and creeps up the grip tape toward the nose, and the board rises right along with it, as if the shoe were pulling it on a string. When the shoe reaches the curve of the nose, the board is at its highest.
look.prompt: Stand on grass and practice only the front-foot slide, slowly. What part of your shoe touches the grip tape?

check.q: Which part of the front shoe brushes up the grip tape?
choices: The outside edge, on the little-toe side
The tip of the big toe only
check.why: Rolling the ankle a little lets the outside edge of the shoe drag up the grip tape.

check.q: What force lets the front foot pull the board upward?
choices: Friction between the shoe and the grip tape
check.why: Rough grip tape creates friction, so the board moves up along with the dragging shoe.

check.q: What happens if the front foot slides too early, before the pop?
choices: The board goes higher than usual
check.why: The slide must follow the pop. Sliding first keeps weight on the front of the board, so the nose stays down.

lessons.title: Jump and Pull Your Knees Up
lessons.mainIdea: After the pop, jump straight up and lift both knees toward your chest so the board has room to rise.
reading: The board can only rise as high as your feet let it. So after the pop, jump straight up and pull your knees toward your chest. The back knee comes up quickly so the tail can rise. The front knee comes up as the front foot slides. Your feet stay light on the board without stomping on it.

Jump up, not forward. When you are rolling, you and the board both move forward. Your body keeps that forward motion through the air on its own. This is *inertia*, the way a moving object keeps moving the same way unless a force changes it. If you also jump forward, you land in front of the board.

While you are in the air, gravity pulls you down the whole time. Your *center of mass*, the balance point of your body, rises and then falls in a smooth arch. Each move must happen fast, because an ollie lasts only a fraction of a second.

You can work out how long. For an ollie of height h, time in the air = 2 × √(2h ÷ g), with g = 9.8 m/s². For a 0.30 m ollie: 2 × 0.30 = 0.60. Then 0.60 ÷ 9.8 ≈ 0.061. The square root of 0.061 is about 0.247. Finally 2 × 0.247 ≈ 0.49 seconds, about half a second.

words.d: the way an object keeps moving the same way, or stays still, unless a force changes it
the balance point of a body or object, where its mass acts as if it were gathered

look.title: Time in the Air
look.cite: Worked example with g = 9.8 m/s²: time = 2 × √(2h ÷ g)
look.prompt: How much longer is a 0.30 m ollie in the air than a 0.10 m ollie? Show the subtraction.

check.q: Why should you pull your knees up after the pop?
choices: To give the board room to rise
To stop the board from rolling
To push the nose into the ground
check.why: The board can rise only as high as your feet let it, so lifting the knees makes room.

check.q: While rolling, why should you jump straight up instead of forward?
choices: Jumping up makes the wheels spin faster
Your body's inertia already carries you forward with the board
The board stops when you jump
check.why: Inertia keeps your forward motion going in the air. Jumping forward as well puts you ahead of the board.

check.q: About how long is a 0.30 m ollie in the air?
check.why: 2 × √(2 × 0.30 ÷ 9.8) ≈ 2 × 0.247 ≈ 0.49 seconds, about half a second.

lessons.title: Level the Board
lessons.mainIdea: At the top of the jump, the front foot pushes the nose down while the back knee lifts, so the board flattens out.
reading: After the slide, the board is tilted with the nose high. To *level* it, press your front foot gently forward and down on the nose. At the same time, keep lifting your back knee so the tail can rise. The board flattens out under you like a table top. The best ollies level out right at the top of the jump.

Leveling is another lever action. The front foot pushes down near the nose, in front of the front wheels. The back foot rises and gets out of the way. The board turns around its middle until it is flat. If the front foot pushes too hard, the nose dips and the board lands nose first.

Picture the board's path from the side. First the tail goes down and the nose goes up, a steep *tilt*. Then the whole board rises. Then it flattens. Then it falls with you. That order, crouch, pop, slide, jump, level, land, is the whole ollie.

words.d: to make the board flat in the air by pushing the nose down and lifting the back knee
a slant, when one end of the board is higher than the other

look.title: Four Snapshots From the Side
look.text: Snapshot 1: the tail touches the ground and the nose points up at the sky. Snapshot 2: the board is off the ground and still tilted, with the front shoe near the nose. Snapshot 3: the board is flat at the top of the jump, both knees high. Snapshot 4: the board is coming down flat, with both feet over the bolts.
look.prompt: Act out the four snapshots slowly on grass. In which snapshot does the front foot push down?

check.q: How does the front foot level the board?
choices: It lifts straight up off the board
It presses forward and down on the nose
It pushes down on the tail
check.why: Pressing the nose down while the back knee lifts turns the board flat.

check.q: What happens if the front foot pushes the nose down too hard?
choices: The board lands on the tail
check.why: Too much push dips the nose below level, so the nose touches down first.

check.q: Which list shows the ollie in the right order?
choices: Pop, crouch, level, slide, jump, land
Slide, pop, crouch, land, jump, level
Crouch, pop, slide, jump, level, land
Jump, crouch, land, pop, slide, level
check.why: You crouch, pop the tail, slide the front foot, jump, level the board, then land.

lessons.title: Land Over the Bolts
lessons.mainIdea: Land with both feet over the bolts and bend your knees, which spreads the landing over more time and lowers the force.
reading: Aim to land with both feet over the bolts. The bolts sit above the trucks, the strongest part of the board. Landing on the middle of the deck can crack it. Landing on the tail can make the board shoot out. Landing over both trucks keeps the board balanced and the wheels rolling straight.

Bend your knees as you land. Your legs work like *shock absorbers*, the springy parts that soften bumps in a car. When you land stiff-legged, your body stops in a very short time. When you bend, it stops over a longer time. Stopping the same motion over a longer time takes less force, so your knees, ankles and board feel less of a jolt.

Here is a worked example. A 50 kg rider drops 0.30 m from the top of an ollie. Speed at landing is about √(2 × 9.8 × 0.30) = √5.88 ≈ 2.4 m/s. Stopping in 0.05 s with stiff legs, the *deceleration* is 2.4 ÷ 0.05 = 48 m/s². The force is F = ma = 50 × 48 = 2,400 N. Bending to stop in 0.20 s gives 2.4 ÷ 0.20 = 12 m/s², and 50 × 12 = 600 N. That is one quarter of the force, on top of the rider's weight.

After you land, stay low for a moment and roll away. Keep your shoulders over the board until it feels steady. Rolling away cleanly is part of the trick. If the board wobbles as it rolls away, check where your feet landed. Feet near the middle of the deck make the board feel tippy, so aim for the bolts next time.

words.d: springy parts that soften a bump by spreading it over more time; bent knees act like them
slowing down; how much speed is lost each second, in meters per second per second
the SI unit of force, written N; a small apple of about 100 g weighs about 1 N

look.title: Stopping Time and Landing Force
look.cite: Worked example: 50 kg rider landing at 2.4 m/s; force = mass × (speed ÷ stopping time), not counting body weight
look.prompt: What happens to the force each time the stopping time doubles? Check two rows to prove it.

check.q: Where should your feet be when you land an ollie?
choices: Both in the middle of the deck
check.why: The bolts sit over the trucks, the strongest part of the board, so landing there keeps it balanced and rolling straight.

check.q: Why does bending your knees on landing lower the force?
choices: It stops your motion over a longer time
It makes the board bounce higher
check.why: Stopping the same motion over a longer time needs less force.

check.q: In the worked example, stopping in 0.20 s instead of 0.05 s changes the force from 2,400 N to what?
check.why: 2.4 ÷ 0.20 = 12 m/s², and 50 × 12 = 600 N, one quarter of 2,400 N.

lessons.title: Standing Still on Grass
lessons.mainIdea: Practice the ollie standing still on grass or carpet, one step at a time, until the order of moves feels natural.
reading: Start with the board on grass or carpet and your helmet buckled. Stand in your ollie stance. First, practice only the pop: crouch, snap the tail and let the nose rise, without jumping. Do it ten times. Listen for the clack and feel the board bounce. This teaches your back foot the quick snap.

Next add the slide. Pop, then drag the front foot up toward the nose. Do not worry about height yet. Then add the jump and the knee lift. Finally add leveling and landing. This kind of *progression* lets your body learn each part before you put them together.

It helps to hold on at first. Rest one hand on a friend's shoulder or a sturdy fence at waist height. Learning the ollie usually takes many practice days. Short *sessions* of ten or fifteen minutes, done often, tend to work better than one long, tiring session.

Count your clean tries in a notebook. A clean try means all four wheels leave the ground and you land with both feet over the bolts. Watching the number grow shows real progress, even before the ollie looks high.

words.d: learning a skill in small steps, from the easiest part to harder ones
stretches of practice time, such as fifteen minutes on the grass

look.title: A Fifteen-Minute Grass Session
look.text: Minutes 1 to 3: stand on the board and rock gently to find your balance. Minutes 4 to 7: ten pops, no jump, listening for the clack. Minutes 8 to 11: ten pops with the front-foot slide, holding a friend's shoulder. Minutes 12 to 15: full ollies on the grass, counting each clean landing over the bolts.
look.prompt: Write your own fifteen-minute plan. Which step do you think you need the most time on, and why?

check.q: What should you practice first, standing still on grass?
check.why: Practicing only the pop teaches the back foot the quick snap before anything else is added.

check.q: Why build the ollie one step at a time?
choices: It keeps the grip tape new
Your body learns each part before you put them together
It is the only way to ride goofy
check.why: A progression adds one part at a time, so each part is learned before the whole trick.

check.q: Which practice plan tends to work better?
choices: Short sessions of 10 to 15 minutes, done often
Practicing only on days you feel perfect
check.why: Short, frequent sessions let you practice the timing often without getting worn out.

lessons.title: Rolling Ollies
lessons.mainIdea: Once the still ollie works, try it rolling slowly with your shoulders level and your weight centered.
reading: When you can ollie on grass and land over the bolts most of the time, move to smooth, flat pavement. Push once or twice and roll at about walking speed. Set your feet in ollie stance while rolling. Glance down once to check them, then look ahead.

A *rolling ollie* feels different at first. The board is moving under you, and fear can make you lean back. Leaning back sends the board out in front of you. Keep your shoulders over the bolts and your weight centered. Inertia carries you forward with the board, so you only need to jump up.

Start with tiny ollies, just a few centimeters high. Height comes later. When the rolling ollie feels steady, ollie over a chalk line, then a flat stick, then a folded towel. Each *obstacle* is a little higher than the last. A low, painted curb at a skatepark can come after that.

If you feel scared, that is a normal signal, and it is useful. Go back one step. Roll slower, or do a few more pops standing still. Confidence grows from many small successes. Writing down which step felt shaky shows you where to start next time.

words.d: an ollie done while the board is moving forward
something a skater ollies over or onto, such as a line, a stick or a low curb

look.title: A Ladder of Small Steps
look.text: Picture a ladder lying on the ground. The bottom rung is a still ollie on grass. The next rung is a rolling ollie at walking speed on pavement. Above that comes an ollie over a chalk line, then over a flat stick, then over a folded towel. The top rung is a low painted curb at a skatepark. You climb one rung at a time.
look.prompt: Which rung are you on now? What would show you that you are ready for the next one?

check.q: What happens if you lean back during a rolling ollie?
choices: The board shoots out in front of you
check.why: Leaning back pushes the board forward and away, so keep your shoulders over the bolts.

check.q: How fast should your first rolling ollies be?
choices: As fast as you can push
check.why: Rolling slowly makes it easier to stay balanced while you learn the timing.

check.q: Which is a good first object to ollie over?
choices: A chalk line on the ground
check.why: A chalk line has no height at all, so a mistake costs nothing. Higher objects come later, one small step at a time.

lessons.title: Fixing Common Problems
lessons.mainIdea: Most ollie problems come from the timing of the pop and slide or from where your weight sits, and each has a fix.
reading: Problem: the board barely leaves the ground. Fix: snap the tail faster and make sure the ball of your back foot hits the tail. Also check that you are jumping, not just pressing down. A light, quick pop beats a slow, heavy push.

Problem: the board shoots up and stands almost straight up on its tail, then falls back. Fix: slide your front foot farther toward the nose and push the nose down to level it. Problem: the board turns sideways in the air. Fix: point your shoulders along the board and snap the tail straight down, not off to one side.

Problem: your back foot stays heavy on the tail, so the tail drags. Fix: lift the back knee higher right after the pop. Problem: the board lands far in front of you. Fix: you jumped forward or leaned back, so jump straight up and keep your shoulders over the board. Good *timing*, each move at the right moment, solves most of these.

Filming your tries, in slow motion if you can, shows what your feet really do. Compare a good try and a bad try, then change one thing at a time so you know which fix worked. When a try goes wrong in the air, it is fine to *bail*: step off the board and land on your feet.

words.d: doing each move at the right moment and in the right order
to step or jump off the board on purpose when a trick goes wrong

look.title: Two Tries Side by Side
look.text: Try 1: the tail clacks, the front foot stays where it started, and the board stands up on its tail before slapping back down. Try 2: the tail clacks, the front shoe drags up to the nose, both knees lift, and the board flattens before landing under both feet. The only difference is what the front foot did after the pop.
look.prompt: Film two of your own tries. What is one difference you can see, and which fix will you try first?

check.q: The board shoots up and stands almost straight on its tail. What is the fix?
choices: Slide the front foot farther toward the nose and push it down to level
Move the back foot to the middle of the deck
check.why: A board that stands up means the front foot did not slide far enough or push the nose down.

check.q: The board turns sideways in the air. What should you check?
choices: That your shoulders point along the board and you snap straight down
check.why: Twisted shoulders or a sideways snap twist the board, so line the shoulders up and snap straight down.

check.q: A skater films an ollie try. What is the best way to use the video?
choices: Delete the bad tries without watching
Change every part of the ollie at once
Compare a good and a bad try, then change one thing at a time
check.why: Comparing tries shows the difference, and changing one thing at a time shows which fix worked.

review.q: Which list shows the steps of an ollie in order?
choices: Pop, slide, crouch, land, level, jump
Crouch, pop, slide, jump, level, land
Slide, crouch, jump, pop, land, level
Jump, pop, crouch, level, slide, land
review.why: The ollie goes crouch, pop, slide, jump, level, land.

review.q: Where do the feet start for an ollie?
choices: Front foot on the nose, back foot over the back bolts
Back foot's ball on the tail, front foot just behind the front bolts
Front foot on the tail, back foot on the nose
review.why: The back foot pops the tail, and the front foot needs room behind the bolts to slide forward.

review.q: What makes the board rise when the tail strikes the ground?
choices: The ground pushes back up on the tail
review.why: By Newton's third law, the ground pushes back on the tail with an equal force, and the board pops up around the back wheels.

review.q: Why does an ollie need grip tape?
choices: Friction lets the front shoe drag the board upward
review.why: The rough tape creates friction, so the board follows the sliding front shoe up.

review.q: Who first did the ollie on flat ground, in the early 1980s?
review.why: Alan Gelfand's ollie was on ramps and bowls in the late 1970s. Rodney Mullen brought it to flat ground.

review.q: In the worked example, why is 600 N less than 2,400 N?
choices: The rider bent the knees and stopped over a longer time
review.why: Stopping in 0.20 s instead of 0.05 s cuts the deceleration, and so the force, to one quarter.

review.q: What is the best first place to practice the ollie?
choices: A sidewalk next to a busy street
Grass or carpet, where the wheels cannot roll
review.why: On grass or carpet the board stays under you while you learn the order of the moves.

review.q: You feel scared before a rolling ollie. What helps?
choices: Go back one step, such as rolling slower or popping standing still
Skate faster to get it over with
review.why: Fear is a normal signal. Breaking the trick into a smaller step builds confidence.
